subject: FEC1A5C44287454E9CA7BCBB4E5EC15C
introduction: These readings say that guidance is the work of the Holy Spirit and not of the teacher: the one who speaks is a reed through which the water of life passes, and what is asked of him is detachment, a kindled heart and the courage to open his mouth, not eloquence or learning. Each of the thirty-two quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Moses slow of speech, Jeremiah's fire in the bones, 'it is not ye that speak', Peter and John the unlearned men, Paul's weak things and earthen vessels, Zechariah's 'not by might'. Five push back or add a side: Emerson's self-trust and Kant's 'use your own reason', John's warning to try the spirits, the Samaritan who heals and asks for nothing, and Rumi's reed, which has a longing of its own.
questions: The readings compare the teacher to a reed through which water passes. What in a person blocks the reed, and what clears it?
John's letter says to try the spirits. How would you tell inspiration from your own enthusiasm or your wish to be right?
One reading tells of eloquent speakers who achieved nothing and of the 'dumb' through whom the work progressed. Paul says something similar. Why might ability get in the way?
A hospital healed a thousand people a year and converted none. What do the readings count as fruit, and what does the Samaritan suggest?
Kant asks for the courage to use one's own reason. Where, in speaking of what you believe, does your own understanding have to do its work?

outside.why: Jesus tells his disciples not to prepare their defence beforehand, for he will give them a mouth and wisdom.
Paul says that we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
Jeremiah says that when he tried to keep silent, the word was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones.
John the Baptist says of the one he announced: he must increase, but I must decrease.

Emerson's counsel runs the other way: trust thyself; every heart vibrates to that iron string. Is being emptied of self the opposite of self-trust, or is there a self that has to be trusted before it can be given up?
The risen Jesus sends his disciples to teach, and says: lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.
Paul says that the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
Kant's motto for enlightenment was: have courage to use your own reason. If the highest truth is reached only by the favour of the Holy Spirit, what work is left for a person's own understanding?
Joel has God promise: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.
Jesus says that men do not light a candle and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that it may give light to all in the house.
Jesus says: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?
Jesus tells his disciples: it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you.
The council marvelled at the boldness of Peter and John, unlearned and ignorant men, and took knowledge that they had been with Jesus.
Ezekiel is told to prophesy to the wind, and breath came into the slain, and they lived.
Jesus tells his disciples: go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Jesus says that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Moses protests to God that he is not eloquent, but slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.
Acts says that when the disciples had prayed they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
Jesus says that if any man will do God's will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God.
John's letter warns: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God. How does a speaker tell the truth flowing through him from his own eloquence or his own wish?
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.

In the parable the Samaritan binds a stranger's wounds, pays for his care and goes on his way, and nothing is said of converting him. Is a hospital that heals a thousand a year, and persuades none, a failure?
Paul says that God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things to confound the mighty.
Paul says that his preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.
The psalmist says: my heart was hot within me; while I was musing the fire burned; then spake I with my tongue.
Paul says that though he speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, he is become as sounding brass.
Jesus tells his hearers: ye are the light of the world; a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
This is the saying the passage quotes: it is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing.
Paul says that he that planteth and he that watereth are one, and that we are labourers together with God.
Isaiah hears the Lord ask whom he shall send, and answers: here am I; send me.
James says: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Rumi's poem opens with a reed-flute that complains of its banishment from the reed-bed, and whose notes move men and women to tears. What becomes of the reed's own longing when it is made a channel?

acts-spake-with-boldness.text: And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness
